blocks.text: Why property manager hours are so high

The core problem is the interruption-heavy nature of the job. You are expected to be available for tenants, owners, and vendors simultaneously. This creates a cycle where you never finish a deep task because a new email or phone call breaks your focus. Studies show that managers check their email 15 or more times per day. Every time you switch from a spreadsheet to your inbox, you lose focus. This switching cost adds up, turning a standard day into an extended slog.
The hidden cost of manual processes

Many managers rely on fragmented systems. You might have maintenance requests in one email thread, lease documents in a folder on your Desktop, and rent rolls in a separate Google Sheet. Manually transcribing these items into a central system is a massive drain. If you have to copy information from an email into a spreadsheet, you are doing work that a computer could handle. This is where the 68 percent administrative drain comes from. It is not that the work is not important, but the way it is handled is inefficient.
Fixes you can use right now

You do not need expensive software to start reclaiming your time. First, implement strict communication windows. Instead of keeping your email open all day, set three specific times to check and respond. Use the ⌘ ⌥ ⇧ shortcut to open your email client only during these windows. This prevents the constant arrival of notifications from derailing your morning. Next, use task batching. Group all your maintenance follow-ups into one block of time. If you handle one request, then switch to a report, then back to a request, you are wasting mental energy.

items: Use Preview on Mac to sign and annotate PDFs instead of printing them.
Use macOS Keychain to store all your property portal passwords so you never waste time resetting them.
Create email templates for common tenant inquiries like lease renewals or late rent notices.
Use Spotlight search (⌘ + Space) to find files instantly instead of browsing through the Finder.

blocks.text: How Lazur helps manage property manager hours

Lazur acts as a voice-controlled assistant that lives in your Mac notch. Because property management requires constant screen interaction, having a way to navigate without reaching for the mouse saves seconds that turn into hours. When you hold ⌥ ⌘, you can ask Lazur where a specific setting or file is. It will draw a circle around the item on your screen. This is helpful when you are deep in a complex web app like Buildium or AppFolio and cannot find a menu.
A better way to draft emails

Dictating your responses is often faster than typing. By holding the fn key, you can dictate clean, formatted text directly into your email client. This is useful for replying to long tenant emails. You can speak your thoughts naturally and let Lazur handle the formatting. It keeps your hands on the keyboard and your eyes on the screen, which helps maintain your flow state.

faq.question: How many hours does a property manager work on average?
faq.answer: The average property manager works a 52-hour week, which is significantly higher than the standard 40-hour work week.

faq.question: What is the biggest time-sink for property managers?
faq.answer: Email triage and communication are the primary time-sinks, followed by manual data entry and document management.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur on Windows?
faq.answer: No, Lazur is currently built exclusively for macOS. A Windows version is planned for the future.

faq.question: Does Lazur automatically fill out my spreadsheets?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or edit files for you. It helps you navigate your screen, dictate text, and provides guidance on how to perform tasks.

fixes.title: Communication Windows
